comments.author: roryokane
comments.text:
After reading the article, I found it hard to remember what the author’s reasons were from reading the tongue-in-cheek section headings. Here are my summaries of the author’s reasons:


I’m a Cheapskate


I don’t like the idea of “paying a service in perpetuity so I [can] think”



I’m Old


Models only handle accidental complexity, but essential complexity is more important

(“I’m Old” is just a reference to Fred Brooks having defined those types of complexity a long time ago)



I Love Mess


I prefer solving messy real problems to confidently oversimplifying them



Friction is a Gift


Friction helps me learn unfamiliar code and guide changes to the code’s architecture

Collaboration, despite adding friction, improves the product and makes the work less lonely



I Care A Lot


I enjoy programming and collaborating with people

I want to prevent consumers from experiencing software bugs introduced by LLMs

The difficult puzzle of programming can distract me from sadness



A Few Other Silly Reasons


The tone of LLM output

Prioritizing my hobby projects

Ethics

Empirical happiness of LLM users

comments.author: facundoolano
comments.text:
I often find myself doing a close reading, pulling up specific files to look over line by line until I understand their context and the choices their developers made. I know I could just ask an LLM to summarize the project for me and save myself the time, but I’ve found I need this process to really marinate in the code. I need it to not just understand the choices the developers made, but why they made them and how they reflect the constraint or idioms of the language they are using.


I sympathize with this attitude and try to do the same, but I worry that the more code is LLM generated the less this approach remains an option because developer intent and purpose won’t be embedded in there to be learned anymore.

Which is an instance of a broader problem: since professional software development is not an individual activity, what has worked for us before may not work anymore if the majority of our colleagues are going in a different direction.

comments.author: iocompletion
comments.text:
This is an outstanding post full of software development wisdom. And at the same time, respectfully, I think you're missing something.

LLMs are quite limited in their current state, and yet they have solved math problems human experts had not. This demonstrates that they can, to a limited degree, do the kind of thinking you seem to believe is out of their reach.

Now, to your point, they aren't doing that all the time. All those 1000's of agents cranking out all that code aren't continuously operating at that level. They are I'm sure losing the ability to see the forest for the trees and slathering on thickets of abstractions.

But the capability to do that higher level thinking exists, and it is only reasonable to speculate that it could get better. It's not that essential complexity would go away, but that there are now 2 kinds of intelligent "entities(?)" who have the capability to address it.

comments.author: Corbin
comments.text: For comparison, a while-loop can solve math problems that human experts haven't solved. There is no secret to proof search, merely the complexity of proof search. It is a category error to suppose that thinking is required to prove mathematical statements.

comments.author: Corbin
comments.text:
Previously, on Lobsters, we discussed Metamath, a system that is extremely amenable to proof search: in section 4.3 "The Anatomy of a Proof", p135, of the Metamath book, we can see that proofs are merely a sequence of instructions to apply to a stack along with a starting and ending configuration for the stack. A proof search is therefore a desired theorem (a desired start and end) along with a while-loop which repeatedly tries to apply every prior theorem to the top of each putative stack, returning success if it ever finds a stack which matches the ending configuration. There is a common question of how to self-apply this system; previously, on Lobsters we discussed Metamath Zero, which can describe itself at a low level and can be compiled to machine code. There is also a common question of whether this is the state of the art; previously, on Lobsters, the state of the art is that we can give a type signature and some objectives to a while-loop and have it genetically evolve candidates which incrementally approximate the desired properties.

The issue really is due to complexity theory and it is not a coincidence that computational complexity theory was first discovered by Gödel while wondering how to search for proofs. If you insist, perhaps thinking is required to come up with hypotheses which would make good theorems.

comments.author: Corbin
comments.text:
I actually raised this question previously, on Philosophy SE, in the context of ChatGPT. My answer is:


Understanding is illusory and ill-defined. Humans merely feel like they understand. Humans may also feel as if others understand, as an instance of the mind-projection fallacy.


I've seen ChatGPT and similar products claim wrong facts about arithmetic, statistics, set theory, category theory, quantum mechanics, postmodernism, stoichiometry, and chemical safety. If they have an understanding then it's a bad understanding.

comments.author: Loup-Vaillant
comments.text:
Well, that part’s not surprising to me. The surprising part is when the LLM finds new solutions, especially to problems that haven’t been solved before. Assuming they’re mostly imperfect compressors & decompressors, an ability to find new solutions suggests that whatever internal encoding they’re using, might actually work at the level of the actual problems & solutions, not at the language surface level.

Like, somehow, LLMs infer the actual problems & solution from their linguistic representations.

In fact, forget about neural network, just turn up Markov chains to 11: full blown Bayesian Engines, whose sole purpose is to find the string of words that is most likely to get the user to click 👍 rather than 👎. My guess is, doing that efficiently (or at all, if being asked open questions), most likely requires internal representations that matches the problem domain, user psychology, or both. Keeping it all at the language level seems wasteful.

Or I could be completely wrong, and that’s why current LLMs are so damn power hungry.
